title: Permanent: sum over permutations vs Ryser's formula
problem_statement: Given an n x n matrix A of integers, compute its permanent perm(A) = sum over all permutations s of {0..n-1} of prod_i A[i][s(i)], exactly (as an unbounded integer). The permanent of the 0 x 0 matrix is 1.

input.size_measure: n^2 entries, small integers in the harness. Costs count arithmetic operations; intermediate values have O(n log(n M)) bits for entries bounded by M in absolute value (at most a few machine words at the tested sizes).

algorithms.name: sum over all permutations
algorithms.idea: Evaluate the definition directly: for each of the n! permutations, multiply the n selected entries and add.
algorithms.pseudocode: total = 0; for each permutation s: total += prod_i A[i][s(i)]

algorithms.name: Ryser's formula with Gray-code ordering
algorithms.idea: Inclusion-exclusion over the set S of columns the rows may use: perm(A) = (-1)^n sum_S (-1)^|S| prod_i (sum_{j in S} A[i][j]). Visiting the subsets in Gray-code order changes one column per step, so the n row sums are updated in Theta(n).
algorithms.space_complexity: Theta(n^2) (a transposed copy of A; Theta(n) working state)
algorithms.correctness: Ryser 1963. Expanding prod_i sum_{j in S} A[i][j] gives the sum, over all maps f from rows to S, of prod_i A[i][f(i)]. By inclusion-exclusion the alternating sum over S keeps exactly the maps whose image is all n columns, i.e. the permutations.

relationship: Super-exponential -> single exponential: Theta(n * n!) vs Theta(n 2^n), an improvement that stays exponential (the V2 check is a runtime fit). No polynomial algorithm is expected: computing the permanent is #P-complete, even for 0/1 matrices (Valiant 1979), so a polynomial-time algorithm would give FP = #P and in particular P = NP. Glynn's formula (2010) gives the same Theta(n 2^n) bound as Ryser's.

verification.method: V1: both implementations agree for n = 0..8 (the permutation sum is capped at n = 8) on random 0/1 matrices and on matrices with entries in [-2, 3]; Ryser alone is also run at n = 10, 12, 15. harness.check is independent of both: for n <= 12 it compares with an exact O(n 2^n) DP over column subsets (a third algorithm, no inclusion-exclusion), and for every n it checks perm(A) = det(A) mod 2 with a GF(2) elimination. Spot checks during development also matched perm(J_n) = n! and the derangement numbers perm(J_n - I). V2: runtimes fitted against n * n! and n 2^n on matrices with entries in [1, 4].

caveats: Tagged T6 (primary) because no polynomial algorithm is known or expected, and T8 because the pair itself is a super-polynomial -> faster super-polynomial improvement. The operation counts treat integer arithmetic as unit cost; the integers involved grow to O(n log(n M)) bits, which adds at most a small polynomial factor in bit complexity.
notes: Contrast with determinant-cofactor-vs-gaussian: the determinant is the same sum with signs sgn(s) and is computable in O(n^3). Mod 2 the signs vanish (-1 = 1), so perm(A) mod 2 = det(A) mod 2 is easy; the hardness is about the exact integer value. For matrices with non-negative entries, a randomized fully polynomial approximation scheme exists (Jerrum, Sinclair & Vigoda 2004); that is approximation, not exact computation, and it does not cover matrices with negative or complex entries. The permanent also underlies BosonSampling (Aaronson & Arkhipov 2013), a proposed quantum-advantage experiment: output probabilities of non-interacting photons in a linear-optical network are squared absolute values of permanents of submatrices of the network's unitary. They show that efficient exact classical sampling would collapse the polynomial hierarchy, and argue hardness of approximate sampling under further conjectures. BosonSampling samples from this distribution; it does not compute permanents, so it gives no quantum algorithm for this problem.
